note: Durable, sourced context for the science behind the mapping problem, accumulated so
later sessions do not re-derive it. Retrieved from official sources only. Where only an
abstract or a data record was retrieved, full-paper review is NOT claimed.

entries.claim: The competition target is geological fault presence, not a geothermal resource label.
entries.detail: The organizer's words are 'structures that are indicative of geothermal
resources - namely, geological faults'. Fault mapping supports exploration; on its
own it does not establish a geothermal resource, and nothing in this repository
claims a discovery of one.

entries.claim: Ground truth for the prize is a set of NEW faults, manually identified by experts and absent from the public USGS database.
entries.detail: These new faults form the test set for the initial prize round. After that round an
expert panel uses submitted predictions to update the labels for the whole region
and submissions are re-scored against the expanded set, so a prediction that helps
experts confirm a previously-unmapped fault can gain in the final round.

entries.claim: GeoDAWN is a high-resolution airborne magnetic and radiometric survey of the northwestern Great Basin, flown to support geologic mapping and modelling.
entries.detail: It supplies most of the official feature bands: magnetic anomaly, reduced-to-pole,
total magnetic intensity and its gradients, tilt angle, top-of-crustal magnetic
source depth, and the K / Th / U radiometrics.

entries.claim: Faults control geothermal fluid ascent in the Great Basin, which is why fault mapping is a geothermal exploration tool here.
entries.detail: This is the physical premise of the INGENIOUS play-fairway project run by the Great
Basin Center for Geothermal Energy, which is one of the two label sources for this
competition. In this setting permeability is structurally controlled rather than
stratigraphically controlled, so the fault network, not the rock type, is the
first-order control on where thermal fluids reach the surface.
entries.source: Great Basin Center for Geothermal Energy - INGENIOUS

entries.claim: The well and spring inventory used here comes from the Geothermal Data Repository submission 1391 (INGENIOUS).
entries.detail: 27,092 inventoried wells and springs inside the footprint, of which 4,118 are
classed Hot or Warm, with measured temperature and silica / chalcedony /
cation geothermometry. This is an ascertainment stream separate from fault mapping,
which is why it can in principle point at faults the fault mappers never recorded.
entries.source: OpenEI / US DOE Geothermal Data Repository

entries.claim: The registration error between published fault traces and the true surface trace is of order several hundred metres.
entries.detail: The lane brief cites ~400 m measured by Hermant et al. This repository has NOT
independently verified that figure and repeats it only as a brief-supplied input;
it is the stated reason for zoning at 1 km rather than at the pixel. Flagged as
unverified rather than restated as a measurement.

entries.claim: The metric penalises a false negative four times as heavily as a false positive (alpha 0.2, beta 0.8).
entries.detail: Combined with the 300 m triangular kernel this makes near-misses cheap and
omissions expensive, and it is why the break-even bar for emitting one more pixel
is as low as 0.2 x DTI.
